analogy.p: Think of the brain as a ship's control room: the **cerebral cortex** is the captain's bridge where decisions, memory and language live, the **cerebellum** is the helm that keeps the ship steering smoothly and balanced, and the **medulla** is the engine room that keeps the heart and breathing 'engines' running without anyone giving an order. The **eye** is like an automatic camera: the iris is the aperture that narrows in bright light, the lens is the focusing ring that gets fatter or thinner, and the retina is the sensor that sends the picture to the control room along the optic nerve. The analogy breaks down because a camera lens moves backwards and forwards to focus, whereas the eye lens changes its own shape, and a ship's crew can be replaced easily whereas neurones in the brain cannot.
analogy.t: A control room and a camera

bullets: **Brain**: know the **cerebral cortex, cerebellum and medulla** and what each one does.
**Investigating the brain**: studying patients with **brain damage**, **electrically stimulating** the brain, and **MRI scanning**.
**Brain treatment**: explain why brain surgery and treating brain disease is hard (complexity, delicacy, risk).
**Eye structure**: retina, optic nerve, sclera, cornea, iris, ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments and lens.
**Eye as a reflex**: the **pupil reflex** in bright and dim light (control of the amount of light entering).
**Accommodation**: how the lens changes shape to focus on near and distant objects.
**Defects**: **myopia** (short sight), **hyperopia** (long sight), **colour blindness** and **cataracts**, with treatments such as **concave and convex lenses**, contact lenses and laser surgery.
Typical marks: 1 to 2 marks for naming functions, 3 to 4 marks for explaining a reflex or accommodation, 6 marks for evaluating a technique or treatment.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know (Biology only)
core.p: AQA 8461 (Biology only, Homeostasis and response) expects you to describe the **structure and function of the main regions of the human brain**, to explain how scientists **investigate brain function**, and to explain why **treating brain disorders is so difficult**. It then moves on to the **eye**: you must label its structure, explain the **function of each part**, explain how the eye **adapts to bright and dim light** and **focuses on near and distant objects**, and describe **eye defects and how they are treated**. Examiners love this topic because it is full of cause-and-effect chains, and a labelled diagram plus a clear explanation can earn full marks.

bullets: The brain has **three regions you must know**: the cerebral cortex, the cerebellum and the medulla.
Each region has **specialised functions**, but they all work together by sending electrical impulses along neurones.
The brain controls **both voluntary actions** (decided consciously, e.g. kicking a ball) and **unconscious actions** (e.g. heartbeat).
Neurones in the brain make an enormous number of **connections (synapses)**, which is why the brain is able to learn and store memories.
Remember the pathway: **stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → CNS (brain/spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector → response**.
In a **reflex**, the pathway usually bypasses the conscious part of the brain, which makes it faster (link to reflex arcs).
The word **'coordinator'** is used for the CNS: it receives information and coordinates the response.
core.h: The brain as part of the central nervous system
core.p: The **central nervous system (CNS)** is made up of the **brain and the spinal cord**. The brain contains billions of **neurones** (nerve cells) that are connected to each other in a huge network, and it is the **control centre** that processes information from the receptors and coordinates the response. Information arrives along **sensory neurones**, is processed in the CNS, and instructions leave along **motor neurones** to the effectors (muscles and glands). The brain is protected by the skull and by membranes and fluid around it, because its tissue is extremely soft and easily damaged.

bullets: Functions to learn: **consciousness**, **intelligence**, **memory** and **language**.
Different areas of the cortex deal with different jobs, such as **receiving sensory information**, **controlling voluntary movement** and **speech** (examples of regions, not required in detail).
It is the part you use to **decide** to do something, to **think**, to **remember** a fact and to **understand and use words**.
The **folded surface** increases surface area, so a **larger number of neurones** can be packed into a small volume.
Damage to the cortex can cause problems such as **memory loss**, **difficulty speaking** or **loss of movement or sensation** in one part of the body, depending on which area is damaged.
The cortex is split into **two hemispheres** (left and right); the left hemisphere controls the **right side** of the body and vice versa.
Do not just write 'thinking' for 1 mark: use the spec words (consciousness, intelligence, memory, language).
core.p: The **cerebral cortex** is the **outer layer of the cerebral hemispheres**, the large folded top part of the brain that makes up most of its volume. It is responsible for the 'higher' mental activities. The AQA specification says the cerebral cortex is responsible for **consciousness, intelligence, memory and language**. The surface of the cortex is deeply **folded** into ridges and grooves, which gives it a very large surface area so that many more neurones can fit inside the skull.

bullets: Function: **coordination of muscular activity** (smooth, accurate movement) and **balance**.
Location: **back of the brain, below the cerebral cortex**.
Works **with** the cortex: the cortex starts a voluntary movement, the cerebellum refines it.
Damage to the cerebellum leads to **clumsy, jerky movements**, loss of balance and difficulty with tasks needing precision such as writing or touching your nose.
Learned skills (riding a bike, playing an instrument) depend on the cerebellum so that the movements become smooth and automatic with practice.
Do not say the cerebellum 'controls movement' only: the key word is **coordination** of muscles.
Examiners often use the phrase **'muscular coordination'**; use it exactly.
core.p: The **cerebellum** is a smaller, tightly folded structure found at the **back and base** of the brain, underneath the cerebral hemispheres. Its function is to control **muscular coordination**. It receives information about the position of the body and the muscles, and uses this to **fine-tune movements** so they are smooth, balanced and accurate. When you walk along a narrow wall or catch a ball, your cortex decides what to do, but the cerebellum makes the movements **precise and coordinated**.

bullets: Function: controls **unconscious activities**, such as **heart rate** and **breathing rate**.
Location: **base of the brain**, at the top of the spinal cord (part of the brain stem).
It adjusts heart rate and breathing to the body's needs, for example speeding both up during exercise (link to the effect of carbon dioxide on breathing rate).
Other automatic jobs linked to this region include swallowing and vomiting reflexes (extra detail, not required).
It works **without conscious control**: you cannot decide to stop your heart by thinking.
Damage to the medulla (for example from a severe head or neck injury) can stop breathing and the heartbeat.
Link: pacemaker cells set the basic heartbeat rhythm, but the medulla **changes** the rate (nervous control of the heart).
core.p: The **medulla** (medulla oblongata) is at the **base of the brain**, where the brain joins the spinal cord. It controls **unconscious activities** that keep you alive without you ever having to think about them. The AQA specification names **heart rate and breathing** as the key examples. Because these functions are essential for life, damage to the medulla is usually life-threatening.

bullets: **Cortex** = decisions, thinking, memory, language, awareness.
**Cerebellum** = coordination of muscles and balance.
**Medulla** = automatic, unconscious control of heart rate and breathing.
Exam trick: if a question describes a **voluntary decision**, think cortex; **smooth coordinated movement**, think cerebellum; **automatic life-support function**, think medulla.
Information passes between regions along **neurones** as electrical impulses and across **synapses** using chemicals.
Damage to different regions gives different symptoms, which is how doctors work out which region is affected.
Reflex actions (such as pulling your hand away from a hot object) can happen **without** the cortex being involved first, so they are faster.
core.h: How the three regions work together
core.p: No region of the brain works alone. A simple action such as catching a ball needs all three. Light from the ball is detected by receptors in the eye and the information is sent to the **cerebral cortex**, which becomes **conscious** of the ball and **decides** to catch it. The cortex sends instructions to the muscles, and the **cerebellum** coordinates the arm and finger muscles so the hand moves accurately to the right place. Meanwhile, the **medulla** speeds up your heart rate and breathing to supply the extra oxygen needed, without you thinking about it.

bullets: **Method**: record the symptoms of patients with damage, then use scans or post-mortem examination to find **which area** is damaged.
**Strength**: gives real evidence about **human** brains, and shows which functions are linked to which regions.
**Limitation**: damage is rarely limited to one small area, so it can be hard to say exactly which part is responsible.
**Limitation**: the brain can sometimes **reorganise** after damage, so the loss of function may be masked.
**Limitation**: each patient is different, and the evidence is based on **small sample sizes** for unusual injuries.
**Ethical**: it is not acceptable to deliberately damage a brain, so scientists must wait for accidents and disease.
Example idea: damage to the cerebellum gives clumsy, uncoordinated movements, suggesting its role in coordination.
core.h: Investigating brain function: method 1 - studying patients with brain damage
core.p: One of the oldest ways to find out what a part of the brain does is to study **patients whose brains have been damaged** by a stroke, an accident or disease and see which abilities have been lost. If damage to one area always causes the loss of speech, scientists can infer that the damaged region is involved in language. Doctors and researchers have learned a great deal about the cortex, cerebellum and medulla this way. It is called a **correlation** between the damaged area and the lost function, which is useful but not proof of cause by itself.

bullets: **Method**: apply small electrical pulses to chosen points on the brain and record what the patient does or says.
**Strength**: tests the function of a **very precise location**, so cause and effect is clearer than with damage studies.
**Strength**: can be done on the **living, awake** brain, so the patient can report what they feel.
**Limitation**: it is **invasive**, needing surgery, so it is only used when the patient needs brain surgery anyway.
**Limitation**: there is a **risk of damage or infection**, and the brain cannot be studied during normal everyday thinking.
**Limitation**: stimulating an area shows that it is **involved**, but one region seldom works completely alone.
Link to evaluation questions: always give one strength and one weakness for each technique.
core.h: Investigating brain function: method 2 - electrical stimulation
core.p: In this method, a small **electrical current is applied directly to a specific area of the brain** (exposed during surgery, with the patient awake and under local anaesthetic) and the response is observed. If stimulating one area makes the patient's finger twitch, that area is involved in controlling that movement. If another area triggers a memory or a sensation, scientists learn about its role. Surgeons also use stimulation to **map important areas** so they can avoid damaging them when removing a tumour.

bullets: **Method**: patient lies in the scanner while doing a task; areas of increased blood flow/activity show up on the images.
**Strength**: **non-invasive** - no surgery and no damage to the brain.
**Strength**: gives **detailed images** of the whole brain and can be used on healthy people, so it can be repeated.
**Strength**: allows scientists to see **which areas are active** during different tasks, building a map of brain function.
**Limitation**: **expensive** equipment, and the patient must stay very still and cannot have some metal implants.
**Limitation**: it shows which areas are active but does not show exactly what each neurone is doing.
Scans have helped to **diagnose** brain tumours and other conditions, and to plan treatment.
core.h: Investigating brain function: method 3 - MRI scanning
core.p: **Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)** is a scanning technique that produces detailed **images of the brain's structure and of active areas** without surgery. The patient lies inside a scanner which uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves. The scan can show tumours, damage and, in the functional form, which areas of the brain are **more active** when the person does a task such as reading or moving a hand. Because it does not use ionising radiation or surgery, MRI is safer than many other methods.

bullets: **Complexity**: it is difficult to understand exactly what each part does, so treatments are hard to design.
**Delicate**: the brain is soft and easily damaged by surgery; operating can destroy healthy tissue and change personality or abilities.
**Access**: the skull protects the brain but also makes it hard to reach, and surgery is risky.
**Drugs**: it is hard to get drugs into the brain because of a protective barrier (the blood-brain barrier, extra detail beyond the specification).
**Limited repair**: neurones cannot easily be replaced once destroyed, so lost functions may not return.
**Diseases** such as Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, tumours and stroke are therefore difficult to treat or cure.
In exams, use the three key words **complex, delicate, risky** and add one specific reason to earn the mark.
core.h: Why treating brain damage and disease is so difficult
core.p: Treating brain damage and brain diseases is much harder than treating most other parts of the body. The brain is **extremely complex**, with billions of neurones making trillions of connections, and the different regions are **delicate** and tightly connected, so it is hard to treat one area without affecting another. Brain surgery carries **serious risks**, such as bleeding, infection and loss of abilities. In addition, nerve cells in the brain have a very **limited ability to repair themselves**, so damage is often permanent.

bullets: **Retina**: the layer at the back of the eye containing **light receptor cells**, sensitive to **light intensity and colour**; the image is formed here.
**Optic nerve**: carries **impulses from the retina to the brain**.
**Sclera**: the tough, white outer layer that **protects the eye** and gives it its shape.
**Cornea**: the transparent front surface that **refracts light** into the eye (it does most of the bending of light).
**Iris**: a ring of muscle that **controls the size of the pupil** and so the amount of light entering the eye.
**Pupil**: the hole in the centre of the iris through which light enters.
**Lens**: transparent, flexible structure that **focuses light onto the retina** by changing shape.
**Ciliary muscles** and **suspensory ligaments**: together they **change the shape of the lens** to focus on near or distant objects.
core.h: The eye: structure and function of each part
core.p: The eye is a **sense organ** containing **receptor cells** that are sensitive to **light intensity and colour**. Light enters at the front, is **refracted (bent)** by the cornea and lens to form a sharp image on the retina, and the receptors send impulses to the brain along the optic nerve. You must be able to label a diagram and give the function of each part.

bullets: **Bright light**: circular muscles **contract**, radial muscles **relax**, pupil **constricts** (gets smaller), less light enters.
**Dim light**: radial muscles **contract**, circular muscles **relax**, pupil **dilates** (gets larger), more light enters.
The pathway is: **light (stimulus) → receptors in retina → sensory neurone → CNS → motor neurone → muscles of the iris (effector) → change in pupil size**.
It is a **reflex**: automatic, fast and involuntary, and it protects the retina from damage by too much light.
Moving from a dark room to bright sunshine makes your pupils shrink quickly - and the reverse takes longer.
Pupil size changes the **amount of light** but not the **focus**.
Exam tip: always say which muscle **contracts** AND which **relaxes**; one without the other loses a mark.
core.h: The iris reflex: adapting to bright and dim light
core.p: The size of the pupil is controlled by two sets of muscles in the **iris**: **circular muscles** that form rings around the pupil and **radial muscles** that run outwards like the spokes of a wheel. This is a **reflex** that protects the retina and lets you see in different light levels. In **bright light**, the **circular muscles contract** and the **radial muscles relax**, so the pupil gets **smaller**, letting less light enter and protecting the retina from damage. In **dim light**, the **radial muscles contract** and the **circular muscles relax**, making the pupil **larger** so more light enters and you can see.

bullets: **Near object**: ciliary muscles **contract** → suspensory ligaments **loosen** → lens becomes **thicker and more curved** → light is **refracted more**.
**Distant object**: ciliary muscles **relax** → suspensory ligaments are **pulled tight** → lens becomes **thinner and less curved** → light is **refracted less**.
Light rays from a near object are **diverging** strongly and need more bending to focus; rays from a distant object are almost **parallel** and need less.
The aim in both cases is to form a **sharp, focused image on the retina**.
The cornea does most of the bending of light but it has a fixed shape, so only the **lens** can be adjusted.
Watch the common error: when the muscles **contract** the ring becomes **smaller** and the ligaments become **slack**, not tight.
Link to forces: tension in the ligaments is what stretches the elastic lens into a flatter shape.
core.h: Accommodation: focusing on near and distant objects
core.p: **Accommodation** is the ability of the eye to change the shape of the lens to focus on objects at different distances. The shape is controlled by the **ciliary muscles**, which are a ring of muscle around the lens, and by the **suspensory ligaments** that connect the muscles to the lens. To focus on a **near object**, the **ciliary muscles contract**, which makes the ring smaller; the **suspensory ligaments loosen**; the lens is no longer pulled flat, so it becomes **thicker (more curved)** and refracts the light rays more strongly. To focus on a **distant object**, the **ciliary muscles relax**, the ring gets larger, the **suspensory ligaments are pulled tight**, and the lens is pulled **thin (less curved)** so it refracts light rays less.

bullets: **Myopia**: near objects clear, **distant objects blurred**; image focused **in front of** the retina.
**Hyperopia**: distant objects clear, **near objects blurred**; image focused **behind** the retina.
**Colour blindness**: inability to tell certain colours apart, caused by faulty or missing **colour receptor cells** in the retina.
**Cataracts**: the lens (or cornea) becomes **cloudy**, so less light passes through and the image is blurred.
Typical causes of myopia/hyperopia: the shape of the **eyeball** (too long/short) or **lens/cornea** (too curved/too flat).
Many sight problems get worse with age because the lens becomes less flexible.
Check which way round: **myopia = My-opia = near is fine, far is not**; hyperopia is the opposite.
core.h: Eye defects: myopia, hyperopia, colour blindness and cataracts
core.p: Eye defects occur when the eye fails to focus light correctly on the retina or is unable to detect light normally. **Myopia (short-sightedness)** is difficulty seeing **distant** objects clearly: light from distant objects is focused **in front of the retina**, usually because the eyeball is too long or the lens too curved. **Hyperopia (long-sightedness)** is difficulty seeing **near** objects clearly: light from near objects is focused **behind the retina**, usually because the eyeball is too short or the lens is too flat and cannot become thick enough. **Colour blindness** is difficulty distinguishing certain colours because some of the colour receptor cells in the retina do not work properly, and **cataracts** are cloudy patches on the lens (or cornea) that make vision blurred and can lead to blindness.

bullets: **Spectacles (glasses)**: concave lenses for myopia, convex lenses for hyperopia; safe, cheap and easily changed.
**Contact lenses**: placed on the surface of the eye, doing the same job as spectacles (hard or soft types).
**Laser surgery**: a laser **changes the shape of the cornea**, so the light is refracted correctly - permanent but carries some risk.
**Replacement lens**: the natural lens is removed and an artificial lens is implanted (used for cataracts and for some focusing problems).
For cataracts, **surgery to replace the cloudy lens** with a clear artificial lens restores vision.
Evaluating options: spectacles and contact lenses are **reversible and low risk**; surgery is **permanent** with a small risk of complications.
Know the lens shapes: **concave curves inwards (thin in the middle)** and **convex bulges outwards (thick in the middle)**.
core.p: Eye defects can be treated in several ways. **Spectacles** use a lens to bend the light before it enters the eye, so that the image falls correctly on the retina: **concave (diverging) lenses** are used for **myopia**, which spread the rays slightly so that the eye's lens brings them to focus further back; **convex (converging) lenses** are used for **hyperopia**, which bring the rays together slightly before they enter the eye so that they focus sooner. Other treatments are **contact lenses**, **laser eye surgery** and **replacement lens surgery**.

bullets: **Reflex arc**: the pupil reflex follows stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → CNS → motor neurone → effector.
**Homeostasis**: the brain coordinates body temperature, blood glucose and water balance.
**Physics link**: convex lenses converge light, concave lenses diverge it; the eye lens refracts light to form an image.
**Maths skill**: interpret images of brain scans and compare areas of activity; read data tables on brain damage and function.
**Evaluation**: for any investigation method (damage, stimulation, MRI) give a benefit and a limitation, then reach a judgement.
**Ethics**: some techniques are only used when medically needed, and patients must give informed consent.
**Command words**: 'Describe' (what happens), 'Explain' (because), 'Evaluate' (strengths, weaknesses, conclusion).
core.h: Links to other topics, maths skills and exam strategy
core.p: This topic links to many others. The nervous system and reflex arc topics explain how impulses travel from the eye to the brain, and the iris reflex is a classic example of a reflex action. The brain regions link to homeostasis (the hypothalamus controls body temperature - covered in the next topic) and to the endocrine system (the pituitary gland is controlled by the brain). In physics, the cornea and lens **refract** light, linking to the study of lenses.

exam: **1 mark (State the function)**: use the spec words, e.g. cerebral cortex = consciousness, intelligence, memory and language; cerebellum = muscular coordination; medulla = unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing.
**Labelling the eye (up to 4 marks)**: use the exact names (cornea, iris, lens, retina, optic nerve, sclera, ciliary muscle, suspensory ligaments) and make sure each label line ends on the structure.
**Pupil reflex (3-4 marks)**: name the stimulus (bright or dim light), say which muscles contract AND which relax, and state the effect on pupil size and the amount of light entering the eye.

**Accommodation (4 marks)**: ciliary muscles contract/relax, suspensory ligaments loosen/tighten, lens thicker/thinner, light refracted more/less, image focused on the retina. Give all four links in order for each case.
**Eye defects (2-3 marks)**: say where the light is focused (in front of or behind the retina), name the type of lens that corrects it (concave for myopia, convex for hyperopia) and say why it works.

**Evaluating a technique (4-6 marks)**: for each of damage studies, electrical stimulation and MRI, give a strength and a limitation, then give a justified conclusion (e.g. MRI is safest because it is non-invasive).
**Why brain treatment is hard (2 marks)**: use 'complex' and 'delicate' and add a consequence, e.g. 'operating risks damaging healthy tissue and neurones cannot repair themselves'.
**Structure to function (explain)**: use the pattern 'It does X, so Y happens, which means Z'; avoid vague words such as 'helps' on their own.
**Command words**: Describe = what happens, in order; Explain = give reasons using 'because' or 'so'; Evaluate = both sides plus a judgement; Suggest = apply your knowledge.
**Data and images**: with MRI scans, state which area is more active (using the key if there is one) and link it to the task being carried out; do not claim more than the evidence shows.
**Link to reflexes**: if asked to give the pathway for the pupil reflex, write receptor, sensory neurone, CNS, motor neurone, effector in that order.

mistakes.r: The cerebellum controls muscular coordination (and balance); the cortex starts voluntary movement.
The cerebral cortex handles consciousness, intelligence, memory and language; the medulla controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing.
mistakes.w: The medulla is where we think and make decisions.

mistakes.r: For a near object the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments loosen and the lens becomes thicker and more curved.
mistakes.w: To focus on a near object the ciliary muscles relax and the lens becomes thin.

mistakes.r: In bright light the circular muscles contract and the radial muscles relax so the pupil gets smaller, reducing the light entering.
mistakes.w: In bright light the pupil gets bigger to let more light in.

mistakes.r: Say which muscles: circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax; both are needed for the mark.
mistakes.w: In bright light the muscles in the iris relax.

mistakes.r: Myopia is short-sightedness: near objects are clear but distant objects are blurred because light focuses in front of the retina.
mistakes.w: Myopia means you cannot see near objects.

mistakes.r: Myopia is corrected with a concave lens and hyperopia with a convex lens.
The retina contains the light receptors; the optic nerve carries impulses from the retina to the brain.
The cornea does most of the refraction; the lens makes the fine adjustment to focus.
mistakes.w: The lens does all the bending of light.

mistakes.r: It is hard because the brain is complex and delicate, the risks are high, and neurones cannot easily repair themselves.
mistakes.w: Brain surgery is hard because the brain is hard to see.

summary: AQA Biology-only 4.5.2: you must describe the cerebral cortex, cerebellum and medulla, explain how brain function is investigated (damage, electrical stimulation, MRI) and why brain treatment is so difficult, and label the eye and explain the iris reflex, accommodation and the treatment of eye defects. It matters because it is a rich source of structure-function and explain questions in Paper 2.

terms.d: The brain and spinal cord, which coordinate the response to stimuli.
The outer layer of the cerebral hemispheres, responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language.
The region at the back of the brain that controls muscular coordination.
The region at the base of the brain that controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing.
A nerve cell that carries electrical impulses.
Magnetic resonance imaging: a technique that produces detailed images of the brain, including active areas, without surgery.
The layer at the back of the eye containing light receptor cells sensitive to light intensity and colour.
The nerve that carries impulses from the retina to the brain.
The tough white outer layer of the eye that protects it.
The transparent outer surface at the front of the eye that refracts light into the eye.
The ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil and so the amount of light entering the eye.
The transparent structure that focuses light onto the retina by changing shape.
The ring of muscle around the lens that contracts or relaxes to change the shape of the lens.
Fibres connecting the ciliary muscles to the lens, which become loose or tight as the muscles contract or relax.
The change in shape of the lens to focus light from near or distant objects onto the retina.
Short-sightedness: distant objects look blurred because light is focused in front of the retina.
Long-sightedness: near objects look blurred because light is focused behind the retina.
A lens that is thinner in the middle and diverges light; used to correct myopia.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and converges light; used to correct hyperopia.
A cloudy patch on the lens that makes vision blurred, treated by replacing the lens.

worked.ans: Bright light is detected by the retina. The circular muscles in the iris contract and the radial muscles relax, so the pupil gets smaller. This reduces the amount of light entering the eye and protects the retina from damage.
worked.q: Describe and explain what happens to the eye when a person walks from a dim room into bright sunlight. (4 marks)
steps: Stimulus: bright light is detected by receptors in the retina and impulses pass to the CNS and then to the iris (a reflex).
The circular muscles of the iris contract and the radial muscles relax.
So less light enters the eye, which protects the retina from damage.

worked.ans: The ciliary muscles relax, so the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight and the lens becomes thinner and less curved. The lens therefore refracts the light less, which focuses the light from the distant tree on the retina.
worked.q: A student reads a book and then looks at a tree in the distance. Explain how the lens changes so that the tree is focused on the retina. (4 marks)
steps: Reading the book: near object, ciliary muscles contracted, ligaments loose, lens thick.
Looking at the tree: the ciliary muscles relax.
The suspensory ligaments become tight and pull the lens thinner (less curved).
Less refraction is needed for the almost parallel rays from a distant object, so the image falls on the retina.

worked.ans: MRI is non-invasive so no surgery or damage is needed and it can be repeated on healthy volunteers while they carry out tasks, showing which areas are active. However it is expensive and does not show exactly what the neurones are doing. Electrical stimulation tests the function of a very precise area and shows cause and effect, but it needs surgery with a risk of damage or infection so it is only used on patients who need an operation. Overall MRI is the safer method for general research, while stimulation is useful to map critical areas before surgery.
worked.q: Evaluate the use of MRI scanning, compared with electrical stimulation, to investigate the function of the brain. (6 marks)
steps: MRI: non-invasive, no surgery, can be used on healthy people and repeated, shows active areas during tasks.
MRI limitations: expensive, patient must lie still, shows activity but not exactly what neurones do.
Electrical stimulation: tests a precise area and gives direct cause and effect, can be reported by an awake patient.
Stimulation limitations: invasive, needs surgery, risk of damage/infection, only used when surgery is needed anyway.
Conclusion: MRI is safer and more widely usable; stimulation gives more precise cause and effect but only in few patients.
